analysis.one_liner: Doubles federal tax credits and tax-free accounts that help families pay for child care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have doubled the child and dependent care tax credit and related employer benefits, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2024 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill doubles several tax breaks tied to child care. It doubles the cap on the child and dependent care tax credit, from $3,000 to $6,000 of expenses for one child and $6,000 to $12,000 for two or more. It doubles the amount workers can set aside pre-tax in a dependent care account at work, from $5,000 to $10,000, and doubles the tax credit employers can claim for providing child care for their workers, from $150,000 to $300,000. The changes would have applied to tax years starting after 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Working parents who pay for child care and file federal taxes. Middle- and upper-income families benefit most, because the child and dependent care credit is not refundable — it reduces tax owed but does not pay out to families that owe little or no tax. Workers whose employers offer dependent care accounts also benefit, and employers themselves gain a larger credit for funding child care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working parents paying for child care

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the cap on employment-related expenses counted for the child and dependent care tax credit, from $3,000 to $6,000 for one child and from $6,000 to $12,000 for two or more children [S2][S3].
Doubles the limit on pre-tax dependent care assistance accounts from $5,000 to $10,000, letting workers shelter more of their child care costs from income and payroll tax [S2][S3].
Doubles the employer-provided child care credit cap from $150,000 to $300,000, a larger incentive for businesses to fund child care for employees [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, since the bill contains no offsetting revenue; the larger credits and doubled account limits reduce federal tax collections, adding to deficits. The heaviest users of the expanded benefits would be tax-owing families with child care costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offset, so the roughly doubled tax benefits would reduce federal revenue and add to deficits [S3].

The child and dependent care credit is not refundable, so families with little or no federal tax liability — often the lowest-income households — get little from the doubled credit; the benefit concentrates among tax-owing, middle- and higher-income families.
The doubled dependent care account limit only helps workers whose employers offer such accounts, and higher-income workers are more likely to have access to them.
Doubling the employer-provided child care credit is a direct business tax cut, and companies that already claim the credit would simply receive more.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with child care bills, the doubled credit and account limit would put real money back, which matters in a market where care often costs more than $10,000 a year per child. The honest objections are that the bill is unfunded, that the credit's design leaves out the lowest-income families who need help most, and that part of the package is a straight business tax break. It is a targeted middle-class tax cut rather than broad child care relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Marcus Molinaro, a Republican from New York, introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, joined by Representative Sharice Davids, a Democrat from Kansas [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the action history [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not acted on expire; the bill never received a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much from the bill dying. Working families with child care costs got no additional relief and continued paying under the smaller existing credits. The Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have spent, and employers kept the existing child care credit at half the size the bill would have allowed. The main consequence is simply that a bipartisan idea never got a hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no new relief for families

for.name: Rep. Marcus Molinaro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Child Care Act to double child care-related tax benefits.

for.name: Rep. Sharice Davids
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Two additional Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names, bringing the bill's total bipartisan cosponsorship to three members.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record, and the chair never scheduled it.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; bills without committee action do not reach a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors — but it never reached a vote, so no floor division was ever recorded.

industries.note: Larger tax credits and account limits would let more families afford paid care, increasing demand and what parents can spend on child care. Providers' interests here run alongside families'.

The bill doubles the employer-provided child care credit to $300,000, a direct tax cut for businesses that fund child care. It also helps employers recruit and retain workers with children, though the money goes to employees' care.

industries.industry: Payroll and dependent care FSA administrators
industries.note: Doubling the dependent care account limit doubles the pre-tax funds flowing through employer-run accounts, expanding a business line for benefits administrators.
